opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think computer science is still very much worth studying, maybe even more so now. People sometimes look at AI writing code and conclude that learning to program is obsolete, but I see it differently.

Computer science was never only about typing code. It's about learning how to think: how to break a big, messy problem into smaller pieces, how to reason about algorithms and complexity, and how to build systems that are reliable and efficient. Those skills don't go away because a model can autocomplete a function. If anything, when AI generates a lot of code for you, you need a stronger foundation to judge whether that code is correct, whether it scales, and whether it's actually solving the right problem.

There's also the point that AI itself is a product of computer science. The models we build at places like NVIDIA depend on deep knowledge of systems, parallel computing, numerical optimization, graphics, data pipelines, and so on. Someone has to push that frontier forward, and understanding the fundamentals is what lets you do that rather than just being a user of the tools.

And I'd say AI raises the ceiling for what one person can do. A student with a solid CS background, combined with these AI tools, can build things that would have needed a whole team a few years ago. So the leverage of knowing computer science actually increases. The tools amplify your understanding, but they can't replace it.

So my advice to young people would be: study it, but study the fundamentals deeply, stay curious about the math and the principles, and learn to work alongside AI rather than worrying about being replaced by it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I get this question a lot, especially from students and parents, and I understand the anxiety. When they see a model write code better than a first-year engineer, they wonder what's left.

But I think the question itself has a hidden assumption, which is that computer science equals writing code. That was never really true. Coding is the craft. Computer science is the way of thinking: how to decompose a messy problem into pieces a machine can handle, how to reason about what's computable and what isn't, how to think about cost, about scale, about where a system will break. Those abstractions don't go away because the typing got automated. If anything, they become more important, because now you are directing something very powerful, and the gap between people who understand what's happening underneath and people who are just prompting gets wider, not narrower.

The second thing I'd say is that AI is itself a product of computer science. Everything we are building at NVIDIA, the world models, the simulation systems, the robotics stacks, all of that sits on top of ideas from compilers, from distributed systems, from numerical computing, from the theory of learning. We are nowhere near finished. The models are still inefficient, still fragile, still don't understand the physical world well. Somebody has to solve those problems, and they will be solved by people trained in exactly this discipline.

And the third point, which I think is actually the most important one: the tools make a strong person much stronger and a weak person only a little stronger. In the past, a good idea needed a team of ten engineers and two years. Now one person with good judgment and real understanding can do a large part of that. So the leverage of understanding is higher than it has ever been. The question is not whether to study computer science. It's that you should study it differently: less memorizing of syntax, more depth in fundamentals, more systems thinking, more willingness to use these tools aggressively while still knowing what they are doing.

So my honest answer is, yes, it's worth studying, perhaps more than before. Just don't study it as a trade. Study it as a way of thinking.

astra-6.text:
I think computer science is still worth studying because it teaches you how to think about problems, not just how to write code. You learn how to break a complicated problem into smaller pieces, how to represent information, and how to reason about whether a solution is correct and efficient. Those skills remain valuable even when AI can generate the code.

In fact, when generating code becomes easier, judgment becomes more important. Is the system doing what you intended? How do you test it? What happens when it encounters something unexpected? To answer those questions, you need to understand what’s happening underneath.

AI changes how we build things, and I think the way we teach computer science should evolve with it. Students should learn to use these tools, but also learn to question their outputs and understand their limitations. You can spend less time on routine implementation and more time exploring ideas. To me, that makes computer science an exciting field to study.

sol-6.1.text:
I think computer science is still worth studying because it teaches you how to turn a problem into something a computer can solve. AI can help you write code, but you still need to understand what problem you’re solving, whether the solution is correct, and what happens when it fails.

For example, generating a program is one step. Knowing how to test it, how to handle data, and how to make it reliable requires a deeper understanding. That understanding also helps you use AI more effectively—you can ask better questions and judge the answers.

So I would encourage students to learn the fundamentals and use AI as part of that learning. Try building something you care about, then understand why it works. The tools will keep changing, but the ability to reason about computation will remain useful.
